title: Graphs As Topological Objects
notes: Open by making graphs do double duty. They are finite data structures, but they also become one-dimensional spaces once edges are allowed to be intervals. The first lecture is about moving between those views without confusing intrinsic adjacency with a particular drawing in the plane.

title: The First Invariant: Connectedness
notes: Use the highlighted components as the first invariant students can certify algorithmically. A drawing may stretch, bend, or reorder the vertices, but the question of whether one can travel from one vertex to another through edges is intrinsic to the graph.

title: Trees Are Minimal Connectivity Certificates
notes: Present the tree as a certificate rather than merely a type of graph. It proves connectivity with the fewest possible edges, and the moment one adds an extra edge a cycle appears. The numerical test m equals n minus one should be paired with the unique-path inspection.

title: No Separation Means Connected
notes: This slide connects the graph definition to the topological language of separations. A disconnected graph admits a partition with no crossing edge, while a connected graph defeats every attempted cut. The visual test prepares the later continuous version without requiring new machinery yet.

title: Continuous Connectedness
notes: Shift from finite graphs to spaces by asking what replaces an edge path. A basis tells us which local observations count as open, the subspace topology inherits those observations, and path-connectedness supplies explicit curves. The important distinction is that connectedness can survive even when no path witness exists.

title: Union-Find As A Running Certificate
notes: Introduce union-find as a live connectivity certificate. Each edge insertion either merges two components or certifies that the edge is redundant for connectivity. The slide should feel like the algorithmic version of the component coloring from earlier in the lecture.

title: Why Path Compression Matters
notes: The point is not only that path compression is faster; it changes the shape of future evidence. After a find operation, a long ancestry chain becomes nearly flat, so later connectivity queries see a much shallower forest. Weighted union and compression explain the inverse Ackermann behavior together.

title: Closed Curves And Inside/Outside
notes: Use the Jordan curve theorem as a topological promise with computational consequences. A simple closed curve separates the plane into an inside and an outside, and any crossing from one side to the other must meet the curve. That promise is exactly what point-location tests exploit.

title: Parity Test For Point Location
notes: Walk through the ray test carefully because it is the first place topology becomes a branching algorithm. A generic ray from the query point toggles state each time it crosses the polygon boundary. Odd means inside, even means outside, and vertex cases need a consistent convention.

title: Triangulating A Polygon
notes: Triangulation turns a global polygon into local triangles while preserving the same region. Ears are the visible certificate: clip an ear, recurse on the smaller polygon, and count the result. For n vertices the sanity check is n minus three diagonals and n minus two triangles.

title: Winding Number Beyond Simple Curves
notes: Parity forgets orientation, but winding number remembers how many signed turns the curve makes around the query point. This is why it works beyond simple curves. The regions in the diagram should be read as accumulated algebraic evidence, not as ordinary inside and outside labels.

title: Knots Need Projection Data
notes: A knot diagram is not just a plane curve with crossings. Each crossing stores over-under information, and that extra data records a spatial embedding of a circle in three dimensions. The trefoil motif should make students inspect where the projection alone would be ambiguous.

title: Reidemeister Moves Preserve Tricolorability
notes: Explain the moves as local rewrites that do not change the knot type. Tricolorability is useful here because it is easy to test on a diagram yet survives all three moves. It is not a complete invariant, but it is a clear certificate that some diagrams cannot be equivalent.

title: Links And Signed Crossings
notes: For links, crossings between different components carry signed contributions to the linking number. Writhing and twisting describe local signed behavior of a diagram or ribbon, while linking is global and survives allowed deformations. Keep the focus on what is counted and what is invariant.

title: Euler Relation For Planar Graphs
notes: Return to graphs, now with an embedding in the plane. Vertices and edges alone are intrinsic to the graph, but faces depend on the embedding. Once the embedding is planar and connected, the ledger n minus m plus f equals two becomes a strong topological check.

title: Why K5 And K3,3 Cannot Be Planar
notes: Use the two obstruction panels to show how counting defeats impossible drawings. For K5, every face would need length at least three, which conflicts with the Euler edge bound. For K3,3, bipartiteness forbids triangular faces, giving an even stricter bound. These are certificates of non-planarity.

title: Tutte's Theorem: Straight Edges From Averages
notes: End the constructive arc with Tutte's theorem. Pin the outer face as a convex polygon, place every interior vertex at the average of its neighbors, and solve the sparse linear system. The barycentric equations turn a topological embedding certificate into straight-line geometry.

title: Recap: Certificates, Invariants, Embeddings
notes: Close by naming the three habits students should carry forward. Certificates give finite evidence, invariants survive allowed changes, and embeddings add geometric data that must be checked. Graphs are the bridge because every one of those habits is already visible in one dimension.
